Its not. This was caused by a bug in the firmware, not new firmware. Most people, (even a lot of IT/ tech savvy people) don't really understand what UEFI is exactly or the issues with it. UEFI is a specification for a booting protocol (and I suppose API). Created by Intel in the early 00's, it was intended to replace the old "IBM compatible" boot sequence. There really isn't much to complain about, (other than it's slightly more complex than the old boot it someways, although its easier in others.)

Where most people take issue is that Microsoft got Safeboot added to the spec. They then strong armed the motherboard manufactures to implement safeboot or they couldn't use the "Ready for windows 8" (or w/e the fuck it said) sticker. It's all about certification. It is left up to the firmware implementer which non-microsoft signatures they ship will (the spec is only to make sure you run signed content, could do same thing with linux/BSD), and if they let the user disable this feature. Asus, afaik, always does, and the instructions are mentioned in the article. Asus also lets users and OEMs add their own keys if they choose.

To save their language, Canadas Inuit rewrite it
huh, it was my understanding that it was a solely spoken language

Initially Inuit were an oral culture. The missionaries showed up and introduced the syllabic writing system so they could hand out bibles, and ultimately (with the advent of typewriters and such) a roman orthography system was developed although IBM did produce a syllabics ball for use with their Selectric line of type writers and modern computers have no difficulty (providing one has the appropriate keyboard overlay) rendering/printing the syllabics character set.

Currently written material is produced in both writing systems. As you can imagine that is cumbersome and expensive and has led to a general hodge-podge of written material that some can read and some cannot.

The debate has turned into one of demographics. It gets contentious because

  1. at this point in the timeline the majority of older people in the eastern Arctic cannot read roman orthography and younger people cannot read, and are not interested in learning, syllabics because, in their opinion, they have a perfectly functional character set that works and moves easily across traditional (paper) and modern (digital) platforms.

  2. the western Canadian Inuit dialect has sounds that cannot be rendered with the current syllabics set so the further west you go the more common the adaptation of the roman character set.

  3. there is the residential and public schools faction who were beaten as kids by their white European teachers for speaking or writing Inuktitut (syllabics at the time) and are hanging on to it as a part of the culture that the government tried to beat out of them.

There is also a fear that should the writing system be standardized that various dialects will be negatively impacted. I speak two dialects (and function relatively well in a 3rd) and am functional in the roman orthography writing system and do not see this as an issue - I mean really, if you take the spoken English word from England and Canada they may sound a heck of a lot different but they are written basically the same way - right?

Emotions, however, run high and the majority of people in each of the factions have dung their trenches and refuse to come out of them.

Either way, while I'm as close to the modern Inuit culture as one can reasonably be without being a full part of it I've been keeping my opinions within the discussion fairly neutral (I have close friends and family in both camps and don't want to alienate anyone) because it is not my language or culture. If pressed I would say that my personal tent is pitched in the roman orthography camp because I see syllabics becoming obsolete within a generation simply because the youth do not support it - why delay the inevitable?

Inuit person here. Born in Inuktituit, raised in Yellowknife. I was pretty sure we already had a writing system, introduced by Roman Catholic and Anglican priests many years ago. If they want to standardize it across the north, I would personally recommend that they stick with the Syllabics system because it gives the language a more distinct look than the Roman orthography. Sure, you have downsides like some sounds being limited, but those sounds where not used much by Inuktituit speakers anyway, the problem only arising when trying to trans-pronounce some English and French words. This doesn't really effect me much though, since my mother decided to raise me speaking English instead.
